desc:
For a non-negative integer x, let rev(x) be x with its decimal digits reversed; leading zeros after reversing disappear, so rev(120) = 21.

A pair of indices (i, j) with i < j is nice if nums[i] + rev(nums[j]) == nums[j] + rev(nums[i]). Return the number of nice pairs.

For example, [42, 11, 1, 97] has 2 nice pairs: (42, 97) and (11, 1).
hints: Trying all pairs is O(n2). Look at the condition: can you move everything about nums[i] to one side and everything about nums[j] to the other?
Rearranged, the condition says nums[i] - rev(nums[i]) == nums[j] - rev(nums[j]).
Compute key = x - rev(x) for every element. Two elements form a nice pair exactly when their keys are equal, so count equal keys with a hash map.
editorial: Subtract rev(nums[i]) + nums[j] from both sides of the condition and it becomes nums[i] - rev(nums[i]) == nums[j] - rev(nums[j]). The problem is therefore the same as counting pairs of equal keys, where the key of an element is x - rev(x).

Process the array left to right with a map from key to number of earlier elements with that key; each new element forms that many new pairs, then increments its key's count. Reversing a number costs O(log x), so the total is O(n log M) time and O(n) space.
